scenes.heading: Interior angles of polygons
scenes.say: A soccer ball is stitched from pentagons and hexagons. How big are their corners? One simple rule gives the total of the angles inside any polygon at all.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Cut a polygon pizza into slices from one corner
scenes.science: An n-sided polygon splits into n − 2 triangles
scenes.breaks: you'd cut a real pizza from the middle. Here you must cut from one corner, or extra angles get counted.
scenes.say: Imagine a pizza shaped like a polygon. Stand at one corner and cut straight to every other corner you can reach. You get a fan of triangles. Each triangle holds one hundred and eighty degrees. Just remember to cut from a corner, not the middle, or you'll count extra angles.
scenes.caption: Stand at one corner and cut straight to every other corner. You get a fan of triangles, each holding 180°. Cut from a corner, not the middle, or you'll count extra angles.

scenes.heading: Fan out from one corner
scenes.say: Here is a hexagon. From corner A, draw diagonals to every corner you can reach. You get four triangles, so the angles add to four times one hundred and eighty, which is seven hundred and twenty degrees.
scenes.caption: From corner A, draw diagonals to every corner you can reach. You get 4 triangles, so the angles add to 4 × 180° = 720°.

scenes.heading: The angle sum rule
scenes.say: From one corner, you can't cut to that corner itself or its two neighbours. So an n-sided polygon makes n minus two triangles. The angle sum is n minus two, times one hundred and eighty degrees. Sides minus two, times one eighty.
scenes.caption: From one corner, you can't cut to itself or its two neighbours. So n sides make n − 2 triangles, and the angle sum is (n − 2) × 180°.

scenes.heading: Count up in 180s
scenes.say: Triangle, one hundred and eighty. Quadrilateral, three hundred and sixty. Pentagon, five hundred and forty. Hexagon, seven hundred and twenty. Each extra side adds one more triangle, so one hundred and eighty more degrees.
scenes.caption: Triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°. Each extra side adds one more triangle: 180° more.

scenes.heading: Finding a missing angle
scenes.say: This pentagon has four angles given and one missing. A pentagon makes three triangles, so its angles add to five hundred and forty. The four known angles add to four hundred and twenty, so x is one hundred and twenty.
scenes.caption: A pentagon makes 3 triangles, so its angles add to 540°. The four known angles add to 420°, so x = 540 − 420 = 120.

scenes.heading: Regular dodecagon
scenes.question: Find each interior angle of a regular dodecagon (12 sides).
scenes.say: A regular polygon has all angles equal. A dodecagon has twelve sides, so the sum is ten times one hundred and eighty, which is one thousand eight hundred degrees. Share it between twelve equal angles: each one is one hundred and fifty degrees.
scenes.caption: A dodecagon has 12 sides, so the sum is 10 × 180 = 1800°. Share it between 12 equal angles: each one is 150°.

scenes.heading: Working backwards
scenes.question: A polygon's interior angles add to 1440°. How many sides does it have?
scenes.say: Now backwards. The angles add to one thousand four hundred and forty. Divide by one hundred and eighty: that's eight triangles. Then add two, and you get ten sides. It's a decagon. Divide, then add two!
scenes.caption: The angles add to 1440°. Divide by 180: 8 triangles. Add 2: 10 sides, a decagon. Divide, then add 2!

points: Regular: divide the sum by n
scenes.say: Quick recap. An n-sided polygon splits into n minus two triangles, so the angle sum is n minus two, times one hundred and eighty. For a regular polygon, divide the sum by n. To work backwards, divide by one hundred and eighty, then add two. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: n sides make n − 2 triangles, so the angle sum is (n − 2) × 180°. Regular polygon: divide by n. Backwards: ÷ 180, then + 2. Now try the practice questions!
